lead: A diode is a two-terminal device that lets current pass easily one way and blocks it the other. It exists because of a junction between two differently doped pieces of silicon. Below about 0.7 V forward it conducts almost nothing; above that the current rises steeply. This one-way behaviour turns alternating current into direct current, protects a circuit from a reversed battery, and clips voltage spikes. Every phone charger you plug in has diodes doing exactly this job. This chapter builds the diode from the silicon atom upward, then reads its voltage-current curve.
prereq: You need: Ohm's law, KVL and series circuits from Unit 1, DC Circuits and Network Theorems.

blocks.text: Silicon has four electrons in its outer shell. In a crystal each atom shares one electron with each of four neighbours, forming covalent bonds. At room temperature a few bonds break, releasing a free electron and leaving a vacancy called a hole. Both carry current: the electron moves through the crystal, and the hole moves when a neighbouring electron fills it. Pure silicon, called intrinsic silicon, has very few such pairs, so it conducts poorly.
Doping adds a tiny amount of impurity, roughly one atom in a million, to make the silicon useful. The added atoms are called dopants.

items: Trivalent dopant (boron, aluminium, gallium) has three outer electrons. One bond stays incomplete, so each dopant atom gives one hole. Holes become the majority carriers and electrons the minority carriers. The result is p-type silicon.

Pentavalent dopant (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) has five outer electrons. Four fit the bonds and the fifth is loosely held, so each atom gives one free electron. Electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers. The result is n-type silicon.
Doped silicon is still electrically neutral; the dopant atom brings its own nucleus. Doping changes only which carrier is plentiful, not the net charge.

blocks.text: Join a p piece and an n piece in one crystal and the boundary is a PN junction. Holes on the p side diffuse across into the n side, and electrons diffuse the other way. Each hole that leaves behind leaves a fixed negative acceptor ion; each electron that leaves leaves a fixed positive donor ion. A thin layer near the junction is left with no mobile carriers. It is called the depletion region.

The exposed ions create an electric field pointing from the n side to the p side. This field pushes carriers back and opposes the diffusion. Equilibrium arrives when the drift current equals the diffusion current, so with nothing connected the net current is zero.

A voltage still sits across the depletion region at equilibrium. It is the barrier potential, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium at room temperature. It falls slightly as temperature rises. The depletion width is a few micrometres; it widens in reverse bias and narrows in forward bias, and that is the whole mechanism of the diode.

sections.h3: Forward bias, reverse bias and the V-I characteristic

blocks.text: Forward bias connects the p side to the positive terminal and the n side to the negative. The applied field opposes the barrier, the depletion region narrows, and current begins. Below the knee voltage, about 0.6 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, the current is negligible. Above it the current rises steeply and the diode behaves like a fixed voltage drop. The series resistor, not the diode, then decides the current.

blocks.where: I is the diode current in A; V is the voltage across the diode in V, positive in forward bias; I_s is the reverse saturation current in A; n is the ideality factor, about 1 for germanium and 1 to 2 for silicon; V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at room temperature, where k is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature and q the electron charge.

blocks.text: Reverse bias connects p to the negative terminal and n to the positive. The barrier grows, the depletion region widens, and only minority carriers cross. The result is a small reverse saturation current, a few nanoamperes for silicon and a few microamperes for germanium, almost independent of the reverse voltage. Enough reverse voltage causes breakdown; the voltage then stays nearly constant while current rises, which is the Zener effect (see Zener diode and linear voltage regulators).

items: Ideal diode: 0 V drop when forward biased, open circuit when reverse biased. Use it only for quick estimates.
Practical diode: 0.7 V drop for silicon or 0.3 V for germanium forward, small leakage reverse, and a stated breakdown voltage.
The triangle of the diode symbol points from anode (p side) to cathode (n side), which is the direction of forward current.

blocks.text: A rectifier converts AC to DC. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode, conducts on one half cycle only, and the load sees a series of pulses. A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer, or four in a bridge, and conducts on both halves.

blocks.where: r is the ripple factor, a measure of how much AC is left in the DC output (smaller is better); I_rms is the RMS value of the output in A; I_dc is the average output in A; η is the rectification efficiency in percent; P_dc is the DC power delivered to the load in W; P_ac is the AC power taken from the source in W.

blocks.text: A clipper uses a diode and a resistor to cut off the part of a waveform above or below a chosen level. A simple clipper clips near 0.7 V; a biased clipper sets the level with a battery in series with the diode. Clippers protect sensitive inputs, such as the input of an op-amp, from overvoltage.

figure.caption: Silicon diode characteristic. Current is almost zero until about 0.6 V forward, then climbs steeply; in reverse the curve sits flat at almost zero current.

spec.aria: Plot of silicon diode current against voltage: nearly zero until about 0.6 V forward, then a steep rise, with the reverse side flat at almost zero current.

examples.question: A silicon diode in series with a 220 Ω resistor is connected to the 5 V output of a phone charger. Take the diode drop as 0.7 V. Find the diode current and the power the diode dissipates.
steps: The supply and the diode and the resistor are in series, so KVL gives V_supply = V_diode + V_R.
Voltage across the resistor: V_R = 5 V − 0.7 V = 4.3 V.
Ohm's law gives the series current, which is also the diode current: I = V_R / R = 4.3 V / 220 Ω = 0.01955 A = 19.55 mA.
Power in the diode: P = V_diode × I = 0.7 V × 0.01955 A = 0.01368 W = 13.68 mW.
Check the power in the resistor for comparison: P_R = 4.3 V × 19.55 mA = 84.06 mW, so most of the heat is in the resistor, not the diode.
examples.answer: The diode current is 19.55 mA and the diode dissipates 13.68 mW.
examples.check:
V = 5.0
R = 220.0
Vd = 0.7
I = (V - Vd) / R
print(round(I * 1000, 2))
print(round(Vd * I * 1000, 2))

traps: Using an ideal diode with 0 V drop when the 0.7 V decides the current. In the 5 V, 220 Ω circuit above, 0 V gives 22.7 mA and 0.7 V gives 19.55 mA, a 15% error.
Drawing the diode arrow backwards. The triangle points from anode (p side) to cathode (n side); forward current flows that way.
Calling p-type silicon positively charged. It is neutral; the p only means holes are the majority carriers.
Swapping rectifier numbers. Half-wave: ripple factor 1.21, efficiency 40.6%. Full-wave: 0.482, 81.2%. Ripple frequency doubles to 100 Hz for full-wave on a 50 Hz supply.
Quoting reverse saturation current in mA, or saying it rises with reverse voltage. It is nA for silicon and µA for germanium, and stays almost flat until breakdown.

quiz.q: Which are the majority carriers in p-type silicon and in n-type silicon?
quiz.a: Holes are majority in p-type; electrons are majority in n-type.

quiz.q: State the barrier potential of a silicon and a germanium PN junction at room temperature.
quiz.a: About 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.

quiz.q: An unconnected PN junction carries no net current at equilibrium. Explain why.
quiz.a: The exposed ions in the depletion region create an electric field. The drift current this field drives exactly cancels the diffusion current of holes and electrons, so the net current is zero.

quiz.q: A silicon diode in series with a 1 kΩ resistor is connected to a 12 V supply, forward biased. Find the current. Take the diode drop as 0.7 V.
A germanium diode with a forward drop of 0.3 V is in series with a 470 Ω resistor across a 6 V supply. Find the diode current and the power it dissipates.
A silicon diode has its cathode tied to the positive terminal of a 5 V supply through a 220 Ω resistor, and its anode to the negative terminal. What current flows, and what does the resistor see?
quiz.a: The diode is reverse biased. Only the reverse saturation current flows, a few nanoamperes, so it is effectively zero; the whole 5 V appears across the diode, and the resistor sees no measurable drop. If 5 V exceeded the breakdown rating, the diode would conduct in breakdown instead.

quiz.q: Half-wave and full-wave rectifiers are both fed from a 50 Hz supply. Compare output ripple frequency, ripple factor and efficiency, and say which gives the smoother DC.
quiz.a: Half-wave: 50 Hz ripple, ripple factor 1.21, efficiency 40.6%. Full-wave: 100 Hz ripple, ripple factor 0.482, efficiency 81.2%. Two output pulses per cycle make the full-wave output smoother and easier to filter, so it is preferred in practice.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plain silicon PN diodes rarely rectify in modern chargers: Schottky diodes switch faster with a lower forward drop, and wide-bandgap materials such as silicon carbide and gallium nitride hold off hundreds of volts at high switching frequency, which is why laptop chargers have shrunk so much. The same junction physics runs the light-emitting diodes in your room and the perovskite solar cells in research labs. Useful search terms: Schottky barrier diode, SiC power diode, power factor correction boost converter.
